rationale: B wins because it is more disciplined about what can actually survive contact with a reporter: “Honestly weak. The study is ongoing with no results...” is the kind of kill switch founders need before they embarrass themselves. A has the punchier line, “Your mattress now watches your blood oxygen. Doctors have questions,” but it decorates strong angles with unsupported claims like “sleep apnea... affects tens of millions” and “$3,000 mattress.” Good angle, loose hands.
gaps_in_A: “sleep apnea... affects tens of millions of adults, most undiagnosed” imports an unsourced statistic and clinical context not supplied in the update.
“On a $3,000 mattress” invents a price; the update only says the product costs several thousand dollars.
“consumer health companies routinely commission studies designed to validate features rather than test them” is a useful suspicion, not a fact from this update.
“draws FDA warning letters” is too confident without regulatory precedent or counsel-backed evidence in the supplied facts.
gaps_in_B: “Snoring detection lands in the biohacker bed before it lands in the sleep clinic” is overcooked and arguably false; sleep clinics already live in snoring-and-oxygen territory.
“CPAP makers and home sleep-test vendors own the snoring-and-oxygen territory” brings in an external market frame the update does not establish.
“the sensors ship in the hardware” is probably inferable, but still needs confirmation before a paywall angle leans on it.
The first angle is mislabeled “category-creation” when it is plainly a regulatory/wellness-boundary story. Small wound, but sloppy labeling makes targeting worse.
